A synthetic is something that has been made by humans through chemical processes, rather than something that comes directly from nature.

When you pick cotton from a plant, that's natural. When scientists create a material in a laboratory or factory by combining and transforming chemicals — something that wouldn't exist without human intervention — the result is a synthetic.

A synthetic is defined by two things:

  1. It is made, not found. It doesn't come from a plant, animal, or mineral in its finished form. Humans have to construct it, usually by chemically combining simpler substances.
  2. It mimics or replaces something natural, or fills a need that nothing natural could. Most synthetics were invented because the natural version was too expensive, too rare, too fragile, or simply didn't exist.

• Nylon and polyester are synthetics. Your jacket might say "100% polyester" — that means it contains no natural fiber like cotton or wool. The fabric was engineered in a lab.
  • Synthetic rubber is used in car tyres and gloves. It was invented because natural rubber (from rubber trees) couldn't meet global demand.
  • Synthetic diamonds are real diamonds in every chemical sense — but they were grown in a machine, not formed deep in the earth over millions of years.
  • Synthetic motor oil (like Mobil 1) is engineered lubricant, as opposed to conventional oil that comes more directly from crude petroleum.
  • Synthetic drugs are medicines or substances chemically manufactured in a lab, rather than extracted from plants or animals. Aspirin, for example, is a synthetic.

In real usage, you'll encounter the plural — "synthetics" — far more often than the singular.

  • "Avoid synthetics if you have sensitive skin — stick to natural fabrics."
  • "The sportswear industry is dominated by synthetics like polyester and spandex."
  • "He prefers synthetics over natural fibres because they dry faster."

The singular "a synthetic" is grammatically correct but less common in everyday speech. You'd hear it in a more technical or deliberate context:

  • "Nylon was the first true synthetic."
  • "This stone is a synthetic, not a natural emerald."
Natural vs. Synthetic — The Contrast That Defines the Word

Understanding "synthetic" (noun) is really about understanding its contrast with "natural":

NaturalSynthetic counterpart
Cotton, wool, silkPolyester, nylon, acrylic
Natural rubberSynthetic rubber (neoprene)
Mined diamondsLab-grown diamonds
Morphine (from poppy)Fentanyl (made in a lab)
Conventional motor oilSynthetic motor oil

The natural version exists in the world on its own. The synthetic was designed and manufactured.
A Critical Nuance: "Synthetic" Doesn't Mean Fake or Inferior

This is one of the most important things to understand.

A synthetic diamond is chemically identical to a mined diamond — same crystal structure, same hardness, same appearance. It's not a "fake" diamond; it's a real diamond that was made rather than mined. The word "synthetic" tells you about its origin, not its quality.

Similarly, synthetic motor oil often outperforms conventional oil. Synthetic fabrics like Gore-Tex offer waterproofing that no natural fabric can match.

However, in some contexts — especially with food, medicine, or gemstones — people do associate "synthetic" with something lesser, a substitute, or an imitation. This is a cultural/emotional connotation, not a factual one. Whether a synthetic is better or worse than its natural counterpart depends entirely on the context and what you need it for.

• Chemistry & pharmacology: A synthetic is a compound manufactured through chemical synthesis — built molecule by molecule in a lab. This distinguishes it from natural compounds extracted from living organisms.
  • Finance: "Synthetics" refers to financial instruments (like certain derivatives) that replicate the behaviour of other assets without being those assets directly — the same logic of "engineered to behave like the real thing."
  • Music: A "synthetic" can loosely refer to sounds produced electronically (synthesisers), though "synth" is the more common noun in this context.
  • Biology/AI: You may hear about "synthetic biology" (engineering living organisms) or "synthetic data" (data generated by computers to simulate real data). The noun "a synthetic" in these fields follows the same core logic — human-made to replicate or substitute for something real.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

A synthetic (noun) = a human-made substance or material, typically produced through chemical processes, that serves as an alternative to or imitation of something natural, or fills a need that no natural material could.

It's not about being fake. It's about being constructed by humans rather than produced by nature.

When you hear "synthetics" in everyday life, the most common context is materials and fabrics — the nylon in your umbrella, the spandex in your gym wear, the acrylic in your carpet. But the word applies just as accurately to rubber, medicine, gemstones, oil, and far beyond.
